claim: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is critical for associating initially neutral cues with appetitive and aversive stimuli.
source: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is critical for associating initially neutral cues with appetitive and aversive stimuli and receives dense neuromodulatory acetylcholine (ACh) projections.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Baxter and Murray, 2002; Janak and Tye, 2015; LeDoux et al., 1990) in the Introduction section.

claim: The BLA receives dense neuromodulatory acetylcholine (ACh) projections.
source: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is critical for associating initially neutral cues with appetitive and aversive stimuli and receives dense neuromodulatory acetylcholine (ACh) projections.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations (Woolf, 1991; Zaborszky et al., 2012) in the Introduction.

claim: ACh levels in the BLA increased sharply in response to reward-related events during cue-reward learning.
source: We found that ACh levels and nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) cholinergic terminal activity in the BLA (NBM-BLA) increased sharply in response to reward-related events and shifted as mice learned the cue-reward contingency.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from fiber photometry recordings using the ACh3.0 sensor shown in Figure 2.

claim: NBM cholinergic terminal activity in the BLA increased sharply in response to reward-related events during cue-reward learning.
source: We found that ACh levels and nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) cholinergic terminal activity in the BLA (NBM-BLA) increased sharply in response to reward-related events and shifted as mice learned the cue-reward contingency.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from fiber photometry recordings of NBM-BLA terminal fibers shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: ACh levels in the BLA shifted as mice learned the cue-reward contingency.
source: We found that ACh levels and nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) cholinergic terminal activity in the BLA (NBM-BLA) increased sharply in response to reward-related events and shifted as mice learned the cue-reward contingency.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 2D-E, demonstrating changes in ACh release patterns across training phases.

claim: BLA CaMKIIα neuron activity followed reward retrieval and moved to the reward-predictive cue after task acquisition.
source: BLA CaMKIIα neuron activity followed reward retrieval and moved to the reward-predictive cue after task acquisition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from fiber photometry recordings of CaMKIIα neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: Optical stimulation of cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fibers led to a quicker acquisition of the cue-reward contingency.
source: Optical stimulation of cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fibers led to a quicker acquisition of the cue-reward contingency.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4E-F, demonstrating that ChR2 mice earned more rewards and made fewer incorrect nose pokes during training.

claim: BLA ACh signaling carries important information about salient events in cue-reward learning.
source: These results indicate BLA ACh signaling carries important information about salient events in cue-reward learning and provides a framework for understanding how ACh signaling contributes to shaping BLA responses to emotional stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data showing ACh release patterns during different phases of the cue-reward learning task (Figure 2).

claim: Genetically distinct subsets of BLA principal neurons encode the appetitive and aversive value of stimuli.
source: A recent study has shown that genetically distinct subsets of BLA principal neurons encode the appetitive and aversive value of stimuli (Kim et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2016b.

claim: ACh signals through two families of receptors (nicotinic, nAChRs and muscarinic, mAChRs) that are differentially expressed on BLA neurons as well as their afferents.
source: ACh signals through two families of receptors (nicotinic, nAChRs and muscarinic, mAChRs) that are differentially expressed on BLA neurons as well as their afferents (Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Picciotto et al., 2012.

claim: ACh signals through receptors to increase signal-to-noise ratios and modify synaptic transmission and plasticity in circuits involved in learning new contingencies.
source: ACh signals through these receptors to increase signal-to-noise ratios and modify synaptic transmission and plasticity in circuits involved in learning new contingencies (Picciotto et al., 2012), especially in areas that receive dense cholinergic input, like the BLA (Woolf, 1991; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Picciotto et al., 2012; Woolf, 1991; Zaborszky et al., 2012.

claim: Metabotropic mAChRs work on a slower timescale than the rapid, ionotropic nAChRs.
source: The effect of ACh signaling can differ depending on the receptor, as metabotropic mAChRs work on a slower timescale than the rapid, ionotropic nAChRs (Gu and Yakel, 2011; Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gu and Yakel, 2011; Picciotto et al., 2012.

claim: The nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) sends dense cholinergic projections to the BLA.
source: In particular, the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) sends dense cholinergic projections to the BLA (Woolf, 1991; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Woolf, 1991; Zaborszky et al., 2012.

claim: Optical stimulation of BLA-projecting cholinergic terminal fibers (NBM-BLA) during fear conditioning is sufficient to strengthen fear memories.
source: Optical stimulation of BLA-projecting cholinergic terminal fibers (NBM-BLA) during fear conditioning is sufficient to strengthen fear memories (Jiang et al., 2016) and may support appetitive behavior (Aitta-aho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Cholinergic NBM neurons increase their firing in response to both rewarding and aversive unconditioned stimuli.
source: Cholinergic NBM neurons increase their firing in response to both rewarding and aversive unconditioned stimuli (Hangya et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hangya et al., 2015.

claim: Cholinergic signaling in the medial prefrontal cortex has been linked to cue detection.
source: Cholinergic signaling in the medial prefrontal cortex and visual cortex has been linked to cue detection (Parikh et al., 2007) and reward timing (Chubykin et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parikh et al., 2007.

claim: Cholinergic signaling in the visual cortex has been linked to reward timing.
source: Cholinergic signaling in the medial prefrontal cortex and visual cortex has been linked to cue detection (Parikh et al., 2007) and reward timing (Chubykin et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chubykin et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015.

claim: NBM cells fire in response to a conditioned stimulus during trace fear conditioning.
source: A recent study has also demonstrated that NBM cells fire in response to a conditioned stimulus during trace fear conditioning, indicating that ACh signaling may be involved in learning about cues that predict salient outcomes (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2019.

claim: There was a significant increase in fluorescence representing BLA ACh release coincident with correct but not incorrect nose pokes on the last day of Pre-Training.
source: A significant increase in fluorescence representing BLA ACh release consistently coincided with correct (green line) but not incorrect (gray line) nose pokes on the last day of PT (data are shown from Mouse 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, which displays fluorescence traces from BLA of ACh3.0-expressing mouse.

claim: During Pre-Training rewarded trials, the highest levels of ACh release occurred close to the time of correct nose pokes (NP), with a smaller peak at the time of reward retrieval (entry into the reward receptacle, Rec).
source: During Pre-Training rewarded trials, the highest levels of ACh release occurred close to the time of correct nose pokes (NP), with a smaller peak at the time of reward retrieval (entry into the reward receptacle, Rec).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E, which displays heatmaps of BLA ACh signaling across training phases.

claim: As Training began, the ACh release during reward trials shifted dramatically toward the time of reward retrieval.
source: As Training began, the ACh release during reward trials shifted dramatically toward the time of reward retrieval, likely because the animals were learning that many nose pokes did not result in reward delivery.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E, which displays heatmaps of BLA ACh signaling across training phases.

claim: As mice began to learn the contingency, the peak ACh release during rewarded trials shifted back to the time of the correct nose poke response.
source: As mice began to learn the contingency (Figure 2E + Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, 10 rewards), the peak ACh release during rewarded trials shifted back to the time of the correct nose poke response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: As animals approached the acquisition criterion, ACh level significantly increased at the time of the tone.
source: As animals approached the acquisition criterion (Figure 2E + Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, Acq.), ACh level significantly increased at the time of the tone, suggesting that as animals learned the cue-reward contingency, the tone became a more salient event.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity most closely followed correct nose pokes in Pre-Training and shifted primarily to tone onset as mice learned the contingency during Training.
source: Strikingly, NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity most closely followed correct nose pokes in Pre-Training and shifted primarily to tone onset as mice learned the contingency during Training.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I-J, which displays heatmaps of NBM-BLA terminal fiber activity across training phases.

claim: There was a significant increase in BLA CaMKIIα cell activity following correct nose pokes on the last day of Pre-Training.
source: As was seen for BLA ACh levels, there was a significant increase in BLA CaMKIIα cell activity following correct and a modest decrease in activity following incorrect nose pokes on the last day of Pre-Training (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, which displays fluorescence traces from BLA of GCaMP6s-expressing CaMKIIα-Cre mice.

claim: The activity of BLA CaMKIIα neurons peaked later after the correct nose poke response (~2.5 s) compared to the ACh3.0 signal (~0.5 s).
source: However, the activity peaked later after the correct nose poke response (~2.5 s) compared to the ACh3.0 signal (~0.5 s) and appeared to align more tightly with reward retrieval (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: During Pre-Training, the highest levels of BLA CaMKIIα cell activity followed reward retrieval.
source: During Pre-Training, the highest levels of BLA CaMKIIα cell activity followed reward retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E, which displays heatmaps of BLA CaMKIIα cell activity across training phases.

claim: As mice approached acquisition of the task, BLA CaMKIIα cell activity significantly increased in response to tone onset.
source: Concurrently, as mice approached acquisition of the task (Figure 3C, white horizontal line), BLA CaMKIIα cell activity significantly increased in response to tone onset (Figure 3D-E + Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H, Acq.), suggesting that the recruitment of BLA CaMKIIα cell activity likely reflects the association of the cue with a salient outcome (Lutas et al., 2019; Sengupta et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H, and by citations to Lutas et al., 2019; Sengupta et al., 2018.

claim: ChR2-expressing mice earned significantly more rewards than EYFP controls during Training.
source: However, significant group differences emerged, such that ChR2 mice earned significantly more rewards than EYFP controls (Figure 4E + Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, pink shaded; main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=9.434, p=0.0133), and there was a significant Day × Group (EYFP versus ChR2) interaction (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (11, 99)=3.210, p=0.0009).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: ChR2 mice made significantly fewer incorrect nose pokes than control mice during Training.
source: ChR2 mice also made significantly fewer incorrect nose pokes than control mice (Figure 4F + Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, pink shaded; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=12.67, p=0.0061), suggesting that the ChR2 group learned the tone-reward contingency more quickly than the EYFP group.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Optical stimulation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals did not support self-stimulation.
source: In order to determine if optical stimulation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals improved performance in the task by increasing the rewarding value of the outcome, rather than enhancing cue-reward learning by some other means, we allowed mice to nose poke for optical stimulation rather than for Ensure (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A). There were no differences between the EYFP control and ChR2 groups (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=0.6653, p=0.4357).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Optical activation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals is not innately rewarding.
source: There was no difference between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=0.1311, p=0.7257) in place preference, confirming that optical activation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals is not innately rewarding.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Blockade of muscarinic signaling abolished the ability of mice to learn the correct cue-reward contingency during the Training period.
source: By contrast, blockade of muscarinic signaling abolished the ability of mice to learn the correct cue-reward contingency during the Training period (Figure 5B + Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, pink shading, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, Antagonist main effect: F (3, 30)=23.13, p<0.0001, Day x Antagonist interaction: F (33, 330)=10.79, p<0.0001), with these mice maintaining high levels of incorrect nose pokes for the duration of Training compared to Saline and Mec treated mice (Figure 5C + Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, pink shading, main effect of Group (antagonist) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (3, 30)=25.64, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Saline and Mec groups were not significantly different in any phase of the task.
source: Saline and Mec groups were not significantly different in any phase of the task, including across Extinction (Figure 5B-C + Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B, orange shading, main effect of Group (antagonist) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 15)=1.201, p=0.2903).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: The non-contingent ChR2 group was not significantly different from the contingent ChR2 group during the training period with respect to number of rewards earned.
source: However, the non-contingent ChR2 group was not significantly different from the contingent ChR2 group during the training period with respect to number of rewards earned (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 8)=0.09147, p=0.7700) or incorrect nose pokes (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 8)=0.3681, p=0.5609), but both ChR2 groups were significantly better than the EYFP control group (Figure 6B-C + Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B, pink shading; two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs; rewards earned: Group (EYFP versus contingent-ChR2 versus non-contingent-ChR2) main effect: F (2, 13)=7.254, p=0.0077; Day × Group interaction: F (22, 143)=1.861, p=0.0164. Incorrect nose pokes: Group main effect: F (2, 13)=4.884, p=0.0262).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: ChR2-mediated ACh release does not have to be time-locked to the cue, nose poke, or reward retrieval to improve performance of the task.
source: These results demonstrate that ChR2-mediated ACh release does not have to be time-locked to the cue, nose poke, or reward retrieval to improve performance of the task, suggesting that ACh may alter the threshold for neuronal plasticity for cue-reward pairing over a much longer timescale than might be expected based on results from the ACh3.0 recording and NBM-BLA recordings, which could be consistent with the involvement of mAChR signaling in this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and is an inference based on the comparison between contingent and non-contingent stimulation groups.

claim: Glutamatergic principal cells are the primary output neurons of the BLA.
source: Glutamatergic principal cells are the primary output neurons of the BLA (Janak and Tye, 2015), and their firing is modulated by NBM-BLA cholinergic signaling (Jiang et al., 2016; Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janak and Tye, 2015; Jiang et al., 2016; Unal et al., 2015.

claim: BLA principal neurons can increase their firing in response to cues as animals learn cue-reward contingencies.
source: BLA principal neurons can increase their firing in response to cues as animals learn cue-reward contingencies (Sanghera et al., 1979; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Tye and Janak, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sanghera et al., 1979; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Tye and Janak, 2007.

claim: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CaMKII) has been shown to be a marker for glutamatergic BLA principal cells.
source: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CaMKII) has been shown to be a marker for glutamatergic BLA principal cells (Butler et al., 2011; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; McDonald, 1992; Tye et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2011; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; McDonald, 1992; Tye et al., 2011.

claim: Incorrect nose pokes that triggered a timeout were followed by a modest but non-significant increase in BLA ACh levels.
source: Incorrect nose pokes that triggered a timeout were also followed by a modest but non-significant increase in BLA ACh levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–H.

claim: Incorrect nose pokes that resulted in a timeout in Training sessions were followed by a modest increase in NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity before task acquisition.
source: Incorrect nose pokes that resulted in a timeout in Training sessions were followed by a modest increase in NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity before task acquisition (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–E.

claim: NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity coincided with ACh levels.
source: While this was only a single animal and proof of principle for future studies, we found that NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activity coincided with ACh levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 9F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9F–G from simultaneous recordings of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b.

claim: The relationship between ACh release and NBM-BLA terminal fiber activity was not explained by signal crosstalk.
source: Importantly, this relationship between ACh release and NBM-BLA terminal fiber activity was not explained by signal crosstalk (Figure 2—figure supplement 9H–I), further indicating that the BLA ACh measured comes at least in part from the NBM.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9H–I from a control experiment with a wild-type littermate.

claim: During the first few days of Training, BLA CaMKIIα cell activity after reward retrieval was higher than it was during Pre-Training.
source: In addition, during the first few days of Training, BLA CaMKIIα cell activity after reward retrieval was higher than it was during Pre-Training, and the magnitude of response decreased as mice learned the contingency and earned more rewards, ultimately reaching similar intensity to that observed during Pre-Training.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E, which displays heatmaps of BLA CaMKIIα cell activity across training phases.

claim: Incorrect nose pokes that triggered a timeout did not elicit a different response in CaMKIIα cell activity compared to before timeouts were incorporated.
source: Incorrect nose pokes that triggered a timeout did not elicit a different response in CaMKIIα cell activity compared to before timeouts were incorporated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–G.

claim: There were no differences in rewards earned or incorrect nose pokes between the EYFP control and ChR2 groups during the Pre-Training phase.
source: There were no differences in rewards earned (main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=1.733, p=0.2205) or incorrect nose pokes (main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=0.002433, p=0.9617) between the EYFP control (n = 5) and ChR2 (n = 6) groups during the Pre-Training phase (Figure 4E-F + Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B, blue shading), suggesting that increasing BLA ACh signaling was not sufficient to modify behavior during the Pre-Training phase of the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-F and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Once peak performance was achieved, there was no difference in extinction learning between the EYFP and ChR2 groups.
source: Once peak performance was achieved, there was no difference in extinction learning between the groups (main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=2.293, p=0.1643).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Stimulation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals did not lead to changes in nose poke behavior in an uncued progressive ratio task.
source: Stimulation of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals also did not lead to changes in nose poke behavior in an uncued progressive ratio task (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C, main effect of group (EYFP versus ChR2) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 12)=0.0009814, p=0.975).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Locomotor behavior was not significantly affected by NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activation.
source: Locomotor behavior was also not significantly affected by NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (1, 9)=0.05804, p=0.8150.)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: There were no differences between EYFP- and ChR2-expressing mice in the Light/Dark Box test.
source: Finally, to determine whether there was any effect of NBM-BLA cholinergic terminal stimulation on preference for, or avoidance of, a stressful environment, mice were tested for changes in time spent in the dark or light side due to laser stimulation in the Light/Dark Box test, and there were no differences between the groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–F, unpaired t-tests, number of crosses: p=0.3223; time in light side: p=0.1565).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–F and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Blockade of ACh receptors during the Pre-Training phase of the task had no effect on rewards earned.
source: Like optical stimulation, blockade of ACh receptors during the Pre-Training phase of the task had no effect on rewards earned (Figure 5B + Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, blue shading, main effect of Group (antagonist) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (3, 30)=1.285, p=0.2973) or on the large number of incorrect nose pokes (Figure 5C + Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, blue shading, main effect of Group (antagonist) in a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (3, 30)=1.496, p=0.2356).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: The antagonists had no effect on locomotion as measured by beam breaks.
source: The antagonists had no effect on locomotion as measured by beam breaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, one-way ANOVA, F (3, 30)=0.5074, p=0.6802).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Once all groups reached criterion for acquisition of the cue-reward contingency, there were no differences between any of the groups during Extinction.
source: As in the previous experiment, once all groups reached criterion for acquisition of the cue-reward contingency, there were no differences between any of the groups during Extinction (Figure 6B-C + Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B, orange shaded; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F (2, 13)=0.04229, p=0.9587).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: ACh release in the BLA may be involved in signaling a combination of salience and novelty.
source: While the pattern of ACh signaling in the BLA may seem reminiscent of how dopamine neurons encode reward prediction errors as measured in other brain areas (Schultz et al., 1997), the current results suggest that ACh release in the BLA may instead be involved in signaling a combination of salience and novelty.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented and is supported by a citation to Schultz et al., 1997.

claim: Stimulating NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals during learning enhanced behavioral performance, but was not intrinsically rewarding on its own and did not support responding for the tone alone.
source: Further, stimulating NBM-BLA cholinergic terminals during learning enhanced behavioral performance, but was not intrinsically rewarding on its own and did not support responding for the tone alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The effects of heightened BLA ACh signaling were relatively long lasting, since it was not necessary for stimulation to be time-locked to cue presentation or reward retrieval to enhance behavioral performance.
source: Although ACh was released in the BLA at discrete points during the task, the effects of heightened BLA ACh signaling were relatively long lasting, since it was not necessary for stimulation to be time-locked to cue presentation or reward retrieval to enhance behavioral performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the non-contingent stimulation experiment shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cholinergic inputs from the basal forebrain complex to the BLA are a key component of the circuitry that links salient events to previously neutral stimuli in the environment and uses those neutral cues to predict future rewarded outcomes.
source: Thus, cholinergic inputs from the basal forebrain complex to the BLA are a key component of the circuitry that links salient events to previously neutral stimuli in the environment and uses those neutral cues to predict future rewarded outcomes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Use of the fluorescent ACh sensor was essential in determining ACh dynamics during the cue-reward learning task.
source: Use of the fluorescent ACh sensor was essential in determining these dynamics (Jing et al., 2018; Jing et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jing et al., 2018; Jing et al., 2019.

claim: Previous microdialysis studies have shown that ACh is released in response to positive, negative, or surprising stimuli, but this technique is limited by relatively long timescales (min).
source: Previous microdialysis studies have shown that ACh is released in response to positive, negative, or surprising stimuli, but this technique is limited by relatively long timescales (min) and cannot be used to determine when cholinergic transients align to given events in an appetitive learning task and how they evolve over time (Sarter and Lustig, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sarter and Lustig, 2020.

claim: During Pre-Training, when there were high numbers of both correct and incorrect nose pokes, there was a large increase in ACh release following correct nose pokes, which were followed by reward delivery and receptacle light, but not incorrect nose pokes.
source: During Pre-Training, when there were high numbers of both correct and incorrect nose pokes, there was a large increase in ACh release following correct nose pokes, which were followed by reward delivery and receptacle light, but not incorrect nose pokes (Figure 2C + Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Correct, but not incorrect, nose poke trials consistently showed a sustained, significant increase in fluorescence close to the time of nose poke onset.
source: Correct, but not incorrect, nose poke trials consistently showed a sustained, significant increase in fluorescence close to the time of nose poke onset (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, which uses bootstrapped confidence intervals to determine statistical significance.

claim: A significant decrease in fluorescence was observed for most mice around 2–4 s after correct nose poke, which corresponds to the time of reward retrieval.
source: We also observed a significant decrease in fluorescence for most mice around 2–4 s after correct nose poke, which corresponds to the time of reward retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and related figures.

claim: Recordings from cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fibers showed similar dynamics to ACh measurements.
source: Recordings from cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fibers showed similar dynamics to ACh measurements, suggesting that the NBM is a primary source of ACh across the phases of cue-reward learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F-J, which displays recordings from NBM-BLA terminal fibers.

claim: After sufficient pairings, dopaminergic neurons will fire in response to the cue that predicts the reward, and no longer to the rewarding outcome.
source: After sufficient pairings, dopaminergic neurons will fire in response to the cue that predicts the reward, and no longer to the rewarding outcome, which corresponds with behavioral changes that indicate an association has been formed between conditioned stimuli (CS) and unconditioned stimuli (US).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schultz, 1998.

claim: Serotonergic neuronal responses also evolve during reward learning in a manner distinct from dopaminergic neurons.
source: It should be noted that dopamine signaling is not unique in this learning-related dynamic response profile. Serotonergic neuronal responses also evolve during reward learning in a manner distinct from dopaminergic neurons (Zhong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhong et al., 2017.

claim: Plasticity related to learning has been observed in cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain complex during aversive trace conditioning, such that after several training days, neuronal activity spans the delay between CS and US.
source: Plasticity related to learning has also been observed in cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain complex during aversive trace conditioning, such that after several training days, neuronal activity spans the delay between CS and US (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2019.

claim: A recent study suggested that ACh may signal a valence-free reinforcement prediction error.
source: Additionally, a recent study suggested that ACh may signal a valence-free reinforcement prediction error (Sturgill et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sturgill et al., 2020.

claim: ACh's role in the BLA is to modulate, rather than drive, the activity of CaMKIIα neurons.
source: The divergent dynamics of ACh release and CaMKIIα neuron activity underscores that ACh's role in the BLA is to modulate, rather than drive, the activity of CaMKIIα neurons, and therefore may alter dynamics of the network through selective engagement of different populations of GABA interneurons (Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented and is supported by a citation to Unal et al., 2015.

claim: Neuronal activity and plasticity in the BLA is required for both acquisition of appetitive learning (conditioned reinforcement) and fear conditioning.
source: Neuronal activity and plasticity in the BLA is required for both acquisition of appetitive learning (conditioned reinforcement) and fear conditioning, however the inputs that increase activity in the structure during salient events likely come from many brain areas (McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher, 1997; Rogan et al., 1997; Tye et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher, 1997; Rogan et al., 1997; Tye et al., 2008.

claim: Dopaminergic inputs to the BLA are important for acquisition of conditioned reinforcement and for linking the rewarding properties of addictive drugs to cues that predict their availability.
source: In particular, dopaminergic inputs to the BLA are important for acquisition of conditioned reinforcement and for linking the rewarding properties of addictive drugs to cues that predict their availability (Cador et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cador et al., 1989.

claim: ACh is a critical neuromodulator upstream of the BLA that is responsive to salient events, such as reward availability, motor actions that elicit reward, and cues that predict reward.
source: Our results indicate that ACh is a critical neuromodulator upstream of the BLA that is responsive to salient events, such as reward availability, motor actions that elicit reward, and cues that predict reward.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing endogenous ACh signaling in the BLA caused mice to perform significantly better than controls in an appetitive cued-learning task.
source: We show here that increasing endogenous ACh signaling in the BLA caused mice to perform significantly better than controls in an appetitive cued-learning task.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Heightened ACh release during learning of a cue-action-reward contingency led to fewer incorrect responses and increased acquisition rate in both female and male mice.
source: Heightened ACh release during learning of a cue-action-reward contingency led to fewer incorrect responses and increased acquisition rate in both female and male mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: It is possible that basal forebrain neurons co-release ACh and GABA.
source: It is important to note that basal forebrain neurons have been demonstrated to co-release ACh and GABA (Ma et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2015), and cholinergic basal forebrain neurons that project to the BLA have been shown to co-express a glutamate transporter (Ma et al., 2018; Nickerson Poulin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2015; Nickerson Poulin et al., 2006.

claim: It is possible that both fiber photometry and optogenetic results could be influenced, in part, by co-release of other neurotransmitters from ChAT-positive neurons.
source: Thus, it is possible that both fiber photometry and optogenetic results could be influenced, in part, by co-release of other neurotransmitters from ChAT-positive neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known co-release properties of basal forebrain neurons.

claim: Increasing ACh release in the BLA was not inherently rewarding, because it did not support self-stimulation or real-time place preference.
source: However, increasing ACh release in the BLA was not inherently rewarding, because it did not support self-stimulation or real-time place preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: Stimulating the NBM-BLA cholinergic pathway is sufficient to strengthen cued aversive memory.
source: Other recent work (Jiang et al., 2016) has demonstrated that stimulating this NBM-BLA cholinergic pathway is sufficient to strengthen cued aversive memory, suggesting that the effect of ACh in the BLA may not be inherently rewarding or punishing but instead potentiates plasticity in the BLA, allowing learning of cue-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: There were no effects of optical stimulation on locomotion or responding in the inactive nose poke port.
source: Similarly, it is possible that ACh alters motor activity. However, there were no effects of optical stimulation on locomotion or responding in the inactive nose poke port.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D.

claim: During the Pre-Training phase when there was no consequence for incorrect nose pokes, all groups earned the same number of rewards, regardless of optical stimulation or pharmacological blockade of ACh receptors.
source: In addition, during the Pre-Training phase when there was no consequence for incorrect nose pokes, all groups earned the same number of rewards, regardless of optical stimulation or pharmacological blockade of ACh receptors, suggesting that ACh is not involved in the motor aspects of the task or the value of the reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 5B-C.

claim: Scopolamine-treated animals were seeking the reward, but were unable to learn that they should only nose poke in response to the tone.
source: Further, incorrect nose poking remained high for mice administered scopolamine. This suggests that scopolamine-treated animals were seeking the reward, as in the operant familiarization and Pre-Training phases of training, but were unable to learn that they should only nose poke in response to the tone.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Late-firing interneurons in the BLA exhibit nAChR-dependent EPSP's when no effect is seen on fast-spiking interneurons.
source: For instance, late-firing interneurons in the BLA exhibit nAChR-dependent EPSP's when no effect is seen on fast-spiking interneurons, while principal neurons can be either excited or inhibited through mAChRs, depending on activity level of the neuron at the time of cholinergic stimulation (Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Unal et al., 2015.

claim: BLA mAChRs can support persistent firing in principal neurons and can be important for the expression of conditioned place preference behavior, as well as trace fear conditioning.
source: BLA mAChRs can support persistent firing in principal neurons and can be important for the expression of conditioned place preference behavior, as well as trace fear conditioning (Baysinger et al., 2012; Egorov et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baysinger et al., 2012; Egorov et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 1998.

claim: Metabotropic (mAChRs) but not ionotropic (nAChRs) ACh receptors were required for learning the contingency of this cue-reward task.
source: Similar to studies of trace fear conditioning, in which activity of the network over a delay period must be maintained, we found that metabotropic (mAChRs) but not ionotropic (nAChRs) ACh receptors were required for learning the contingency of this cue-reward task.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Heightened ACh signaling in the BLA improved behavioral performance even when stimulations were explicitly unpaired with the cue or correct nose poking.
source: However, we found that heightened ACh signaling in the BLA improved behavioral performance even when stimulations were explicitly unpaired with the cue or correct nose poking.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the non-contingent stimulation experiment shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effect of increased cholinergic signaling in the BLA is long lasting, and stimulation during a learning session is sufficient to potentiate synaptic events linking the cue to a salient outcome—even if CS and/or reward delivery are presented tens of seconds later.
source: This suggests that the effect of increased cholinergic signaling in the BLA is long lasting, and that stimulation during a learning session is sufficient to potentiate synaptic events linking the cue to a salient outcome—even if CS and/or reward delivery are presented tens of seconds later.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data from the non-contingent stimulation experiment shown in Figure 6.

claim: The abundant ACh input to the BLA results in ACh release in response to stimuli that predict reward in a learned cue-reward task.
source: To conclude, the abundant ACh input to the BLA results in ACh release in response to stimuli that predict reward in a learned cue-reward task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ACh signaling may enhance neuronal plasticity in the BLA network, leading to accelerated cue-reward learning.
source: These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that ACh is a neuromodulator that is released in response to salient stimuli and suggests that ACh signaling may enhance neuronal plasticity in the BLA network, leading to accelerated cue-reward learning.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AAV9 hSyn-ACh3.0 was delivered unilaterally to the BLA at a rate of 0.1 µL/min.
source: For fiber photometry surgeries, 0.4 µL of AAV9 hSyn-ACh3.0 (Vigene Biosciences Inc) to measure BLA ACh levels (Figure 2A-E + Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2) was delivered unilaterally to the BLA (A/P; −1.34 mm, M/L + or - 2.65 mm, D/V −4.6 mm, relative to Bregma) of ChAT-IRES-Cre or wild-type C57BL6/J mice at a rate of 0.1 µL/min.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: A mono fiber-optic cannula was implanted above the BLA at coordinates A/P; −1.34 mm, M/L + 2.65 mm, D/V −4.25 mm.
source: A mono fiber-optic cannula (1.25 mm outer diameter metal ferrule; 6 mm long, 400 µm core diameter/430 µm outer diameter, 0.48 numerical aperture (NA), hard polymer cladding outer layer cannula; Doric Lenses, Quebec City, Quebec, Canada) was implanted above the BLA (A/P; −1.34 mm, M/L + 2.65 mm, D/V −4.25 mm) and affixed to the skull using opaque dental cement (Parkell Inc, Edgewood, NY).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: AAV1 Syn-FLEX-GCaMP6s-WPRE-SV40 was injected into the left BLA of CaMKIIα-Cre mice.
source: For BLA CaMKIIα cell calcium dynamic recordings (Figure 3 + Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2), 0.5 µL of AAV1 Syn-FLEX-GCaMP6s-WPRE-SV40 (Addgene, Watertown, MA) was injected into the left BLA using the same procedure and coordinates but was injected into CaMKIIα-Cre mice.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: AAV1-Syn-FLEX-jGCaMP7s-WPRE was infused unilaterally into the NBM of ChAT-IRES-Cre mice for cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fiber calcium dynamic recording.
source: Cholinergic NBM-BLA terminal fiber calcium dynamic recording (Figure 2F-J + Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8) surgeries were performed as above except AAV1-Syn-FLEX-jGCaMP7s-WPRE (Addgene) was infused unilaterally into the NBM (A/P: - 0.7 mm, M/L + or - 1.75 mm, D/V – 4.5 mm) of ChAT-IRES-Cre mice, with the optical fiber being placed above the ipsilateral BLA.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: For optical stimulation experiments, 0.5 µL of control vector (AAV2 EF1a-DIO-EYFP) or channelrhodopsin (AAV2 EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-EYFP) was delivered bilaterally into the NBM of ChAT-IRES-Cre mice.
source: For optical stimulation experiments (Figure 4, Figure 6 + Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5 + Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2), surgeries were performed as above except as follows: 0.5 µL of control vector (AAV2 EF1a-DIO-EYFP) or channelrhodopsin (AAV2 EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-EYFP; University of North Carolina Gene Therapy Center Vector Core, Chapel Hill, NC) was delivered bilaterally into the NBM (A/P: - 0.7 mm, M/L ± 1.75 mm, D/V – 4.5 mm) of ChAT-IRES-Cre mice.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: Mono fiber-optic cannulas were inserted bilaterally above the basolateral amygdala (BLA) at coordinates A/P; −1.22 mm, M/L ± 2.75 mm, D/V −4.25 mm for optical stimulation experiments.
source: Mono fiber-optic cannulas (1.25 mm outer diameter zirconia ferrule; 5 mm long, 200 µm core diameter/245 µm outer diameter, 0.37 NA, polyimide buffer outer layer cannula; Doric Lenses) were inserted bilaterally above the basolateral amygdala (BLA, A/P; −1.22 mm, M/L ± 2.75 mm, D/V −4.25 mm).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the surgical procedure.

claim: Optical stimulation validation was performed via local field potential recordings.
source: For ex vivo local field potential electrophysiology experiments (Figure 4B), the NBM was injected with DIO-ChR2-EYFP as described above, except mice were 8 weeks of age (see Supplemental Methods for current clamp recording methods).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the validation procedure, with data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mice were maintained at 85% free-feeding body weight for the duration of the experiment.
source: Mice began food restriction 7 d after surgery and were maintained at 85% free-feeding body weight for the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Pre-Training, an auditory tone was presented on a variable interval 30 schedule (VI30), during which an active nose poke yielded Ensure reward delivery but there was no consequence for incorrect nose pokes.
source: In Pre-Training, an auditory tone was presented on a variable interval 30 schedule (VI30), during which an active nose poke yielded Ensure reward delivery but there was no consequence for incorrect nose pokes (active nose pokes not during tone).
evidence: This is a methodological detail shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Training was identical to Pre-Training, except incorrect nose pokes resulted in a 5 s timeout, signaled by timeout light illumination, followed by a restarting of the intertrial interval (ITI).
source: Training was identical to Pre-Training, except incorrect nose pokes resulted in a 5 s timeout, signaled by timeout light illumination, followed by a restarting of the intertrial interval (ITI).

source: Mice were randomly assigned to EYFP or ChR2 groups, controlling for average group age.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

source: The stimulation pattern was 25 ms pulses at 20 Hz for 2 s modified from parameters in Jiang et al., 2016.

source: Optical stimulation was only delivered during the Pre-Training and Training phases of the operant task.

source: Fluorescent measurements of ACh and calcium levels were recorded using two Doric Lenses 1-site Fiber Photometry Systems: a standard 405/465 nm system and a 405/470/560 nm system.

evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the statistical analysis, supported by a citation to Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al., 2020.

source: Data were considered significantly different from baseline (Z% ΔF/F0 = 0) when their 99% bCIs did not contain zero for an interval of time designated by a consecutive threshold of 0.5 s.

source: Male wild-type C57BL/6J mice were injected i.p. 30 min before each Pre-Training and Training session with a volume of 10 mL/kg with the following compounds: 1× DPBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), 1 mg/kg mecamylamine hydrochloride (Millipore Sigma, St. Louis, MO), 0.5 mg/kg (-) scopolamine hydrochloride (Millipore Sigma), or 1 mg/kg mecamylamine + 0.5 mg/kg scopolamine (Figure 5 + Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
